meta.title: Who really said "There Is No Greater Mistake than To Try To Leap an Abyss in Two Jumps"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: David Lloyd George did — in his 1933 War Memoirs, about carrying conscription in two steps. We read the sentence in the scanned first-year edition.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There Is No Greater Mistake than To Try To Leap an Abyss in Two Jumps'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Lloyd George: War Memoirs (1933), on conscription being carried in two steps. The familiar “chasm” versions are later rewrites.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Lloyd George wrote this sentence in his War Memoirs, first published in 1933, in the chapter “Disintegration of the Liberal Party.” It is not an abstract maxim: it is his verdict on his own government’s handling of conscription, which Liberal opposition forced it to carry “in two steps.” We read the sentence in the scanned Boston edition of 1933 ↗ at p. 184, and Quote Investigator ↗ verified it on paper in the London first edition.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: War Memoirs of David Lloyd George
Ivor Nicholson & Watson, 1933 — Volume II, ch. XXIV, p. 740

source.excerpt: They resented conscription, which had consequently to be carried in two steps. There is no greater mistake than to try to leap an abyss in two jumps.
trail: We searched the full text of the scanned 1933 Boston edition ↗ and found the sentence verbatim on p. 184, in the paragraph about conscription being carried in two steps, under the running head “Disintegration of the Liberal Party.”

Quote Investigator ↗ independently verified the same passage on paper, citing the London first edition — War Memoirs of David Lloyd George, Volume II, ch. XXIV, p. 740 (Ivor Nicholson & Watson, 1933).

Wikiquote sources it ↗ to the revised two-volume edition of 1938, Volume I, p. 445. The three page numbers are three editions of one book, not three claims — Wikiquote’s own note records that the six-volume set of 1933–36 was reissued in two volumes in 1938.

The image is older than Lloyd George and he did not claim it: QI ↗ documents a stag crossing “a deep chasm in two jumps” in the Chicago Times of 1873, and an Ambrose Bierce fable of a jackal trying “to cross the abyss by two leaps,” written for the London periodical Fun in 1872–73.
source.excerptNote: The sentence immediately follows its occasion. The “they” are Asquith’s own Liberal backbenchers, whose resistance forced conscription through in halves — which is what Lloyd George is calling the mistake.

author.name: David Lloyd George
author.heading: About David Lloyd George
author.metaLine: 1863–1945 · Welsh Liberal statesman · Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, 1916–1922
author.bio: David Lloyd George was Chancellor of the Exchequer, then Minister of Munitions, then the wartime Prime Minister who displaced Asquith in December 1916. His six-volume War Memoirs (1933–36) are both a defence of his own conduct of the war and a sustained attack on the hesitancy he believed had prolonged it — which is the argument this sentence belongs to.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right. It is the wording and the ownership of the image that get mangled — and one name commonly attached to the saying belongs to someone who was quoting it correctly.

items.who: “The most dangerous thing in the world is to leap a chasm in two jumps”
items.why: This rewrite is credited to Lloyd George in Laurence J. Peter’s Peter’s Quotations (1977), per QI ↗. He wrote “no greater mistake,” not “most dangerous thing,” and “abyss,” not “chasm.”

items.who: “You can’t cross a chasm in two small jumps”
items.why: Bennett Cerf printed this version under Lloyd George’s name in a 1960 newspaper column, and it is the form most often repeated since — QI ↗.

Her 2010 book Third World America used the Cerf wording and credited it to “World War I-era British Prime Minister David Lloyd George” — an attribution QI ↗ shows is essentially correct. She is a well-known conduit for the line, not a claimed author of it.

items.who: Benjamin Disraeli, Winston Churchill, Václav Havel and others
items.why: QI ↗ records the saying also being pinned on Disraeli, Churchill, Havel, Jeffrey Sachs, Walter Bagehot and Philip Noel-Baker, and being called variously a Greek, African, Chinese, Russian and American proverb. None of those has a source; Lloyd George’s does.

items.who: Earlier anonymous writers, and Ambrose Bierce
items.why: The metaphor predates the memoirs by sixty years — an 1873 Chicago Times item and Bierce’s fable of the jackal, per QI ↗. Lloyd George sharpened an existing figure of speech into a maxim; he did not invent the picture.

misattribution.truthLine: Lloyd George really did write this sentence, in these words. If you are quoting him, quote this version — and know that he was talking about conscription, not about business strategy.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is a confession disguised as an aphorism. Conscription in Britain arrived in two instalments in 1916 ↗ because Asquith’s Liberal backbenchers would not swallow it whole — and Lloyd George, writing seventeen years later as the man who had supplanted Asquith, is saying that the half-measure cost more than the whole one would have.

That is why the “abyss” matters and the later “chasm” rewrites lose something. An abyss has no far side you can see. The point is not that two jumps are slower; it is that the second jump never happens.
detailsBody: The sentence has had a long second life in management writing, where it is usually quoted to argue against incremental change — often in the Bennett Cerf wording, and often with a chasm. Both the venue and the wording drift from the original, which is what makes the page worth having: the attribution survives the journey intact while the sentence does not.
context.pull: The point is not that two jumps are slower. It is that there is nothing to land on.

sourcesVerified.claim: The sentence 'There is no greater mistake than to try to leap an abyss in two jumps.' appears verbatim on page 184 of War Memoirs of David Lloyd George, 1915-1916 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1933), directly after 'They resented conscription, which had consequently to be carried in two steps.', under the running head 'Disintegration of the Liberal Party'.
Quote Investigator cites the same passage from the London first edition, War Memoirs of David Lloyd George Volume II, Chapter XXIV, page 740 (Ivor Nicholson & Watson, 1933), verified on paper.

QI documents the earlier metaphor (Chicago Times 1873; Ambrose Bierce's fable from Fun, 1872-73, reprinted 1911), the 1960 Bennett Cerf wording 'You can't cross a chasm in two small jumps', the 1977 Peter's Quotations wording 'The most dangerous thing in the world...', and Arianna Huffington's 2010 use crediting Lloyd George.
Wikiquote's David Lloyd George page sources the sentence to War Memoirs, Volume I, page 445, in a section noting the six volumes of 1933-36 were reissued in two volumes in 1938.
David Lloyd George lived 17 January 1863 to 26 March 1945 and was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.
